claims.text: Neither PlaceOrderLong nor PlaceOrderSplit declares a field; no method in them or NamingAfter.TotalVnd reads a static field or an environment variable. Besides its parameters TotalVnd reads only `private const int LoyaltyDiscountPercent = 10`, declared at class level in NamingAfter.
A C# `const` is a compile-time constant: its value is fixed when the code is compiled and cannot change while the program runs, so it is the same on every call.

A `return` statement ends the method it appears in at once and hands control back to its caller; statements after it do not run for that call. So a guard clause `if (...) return ...;` stops the method, and a `return` moved into a new function leaves only that function.
The `_` digit separator in a numeric literal such as `2_000_000` only groups digits; it does not change the value.
At stage-0, PlaceOrderLong's saving and email steps and PlaceOrderSplit's Save and Notify only call Console.WriteLine with the same two texts; nothing is written to a database and no email is sent.
`string?` as a return type is a nullable reference type annotation: the method may return null. `problem is not null` is true when a string came back.
A `private` member of a class can be reached only from code inside that class.

At stage-0 the repo's tests are methods that call code with chosen values and check the result; they reach PlaceOrderSplit only through Place: BothVersionsAgree compares Long and Split for one valid order (1 × 1,250,000, 2 × 450,000, not loyal); AnOrderWithNoLinesIsRefused passes an empty list.
Enumerable.Any(source, predicate) returns true when at least one element satisfies the condition.

With lines new(1, 0) and new(0, 450_000), PlaceOrderLong.Place returns 'a line needs a price' (its loop checks line 1's price before line 2's quantity) and PlaceOrderSplit.Place returns 'a line needs a quantity'.

A function that does one thing can be named honestly, tested alone and reused; a long function doing several cannot be named, tested or reused one step at a time.

When a block moves behind a name without its steps being rewritten, what the code does stays the same; what changes is how values get in and out: what the block used arrives as parameters, what it produced comes back as the return value, and a moved `return` now leaves only the new function.

If honestly describing a body needs "and", it does more than one thing, even when its name has none; a body that only calls named steps toward one result (a placed order) passes. One thing is about what a function does, not how many loops or lines it has.

When a function gets every input through its parameters and reads no hidden input, the same arguments give the same result and its first line shows what it needs; fewer parameters mean less to set up, unless a value was moved into a static field, which only hides it.

When checks do not depend on each other, guard clauses keep the rest of the function at one level, and this flat shape asks less of any reader, new or experienced: no line makes you remember which `if` it sits inside.
Moving lines unchanged is the safe part; rewriting them on the way (here: a per-line loop turned into two Any calls) is a second change that needs its own check.
Whether extra calls between small functions cost time you could notice is something to measure, not guess; if placing an order feels slow, look for the cause outside these calls first.
In `dotnet run`, `--` separates the command's own arguments from the application's: every argument after it is passed to the application being run.

Written with nested `if`s (each check's `if` holding the rest) instead of guard clauses, the code below the checks goes one level deeper per check; this describes only the nested-`if` form, not an `if … else if` chain, which adds one level in total.

TotalWithShippingVnd is private and takes everything it uses as parameters, reading no hidden input; if it were not private, a test could call it directly with lines and a bool and check the int it returns, without anything being printed.

beyond_scope: Section 5 notes that the repo's split version also rewrote the per-line checks into Any calls, and Try it shows the two versions disagree for one input; this supports outline item 2 (moving without rewriting is the safe part) rather than adding a new idea.

Brief one-clause explanations of `string?`, `is not null`, `private`, `const`, `_` digit separators, `Any`, what a test is and what `--` does in `dotnet run`, only because the quoted code or Try it uses them.
